The Hebrew text even calls her a woman of noble character (eshet chayil), the same phrase as Proverbs 31.

Ruth's Moabite origin is striking because Deuteronomy 23:3 excludes Moabites from the assembly. Her story has been read as showing how faith and loyalty bring a foreigner fully into Israel. She became great-grandmother of King David, and Matthew lists her among the four women in Jesus' genealogy.
textSays: She was a Moabitess, widow of Mahlon, and vowed to go with Naomi and take her God. She gleaned in Boaz's field, appealed to him at the threshing floor as redeemer, and married him. She bore Obed, father of Jesse, father of David. The text calls her a virtuous woman and says she was better to Naomi than seven sons.

interpretations.view: Ruth is the model convert (giyoret). Her vow is the basis for later conversion practice, and the book is read at Shavuot, the feast of the giving of Torah and of the harvest. The rabbis resolved the tension with Deuteronomy 23 by reading the exclusion as applying to Moabite men only (Mishnah, *Yevamot* 8:3).
Ruth is a figure of the Gentile Church joined to Christ, the true kinsman-redeemer, and an ancestor honoured on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers. Her loyalty is held up as a model of faithful love.
The book shows God's hidden providence ('her hap was to light on' Boaz's field) and grace to outsiders. Boaz as redeemer (go'el) pictures Christ, who redeems at personal cost.

Many scholars date the book to the post-exilic period and read it as a gentle counter-voice to Ezra–Nehemiah's ban on foreign wives. Others date it to the monarchy (perhaps for legitimising David's line) on linguistic and thematic grounds. The genealogy (Ruth 4:18-22) may be a later appendix.

strengths: Faith in Israel's God as an outsider
failures: None recorded in the text
turningPoints: Marriage and the birth of Obed

context: Israel's law allowed the poor, widows and foreigners to glean what reapers left (Lev 19:9-10; Deut 24:19). The go'el (kinsman-redeemer) could buy back family land (Lev 25:25), and levirate custom provided an heir for a dead man (Deut 25:5-10). Ruth's case combines these customs in a way scholars still discuss. Moab and Israel were related peoples (Gen 19:37) and frequent enemies. Business at the city gate before elders was the normal legal setting.
legacy: Ruth's vow is often read at weddings, though originally spoken between two women. The book is read on Shavuot. She is one of the four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, with Tamar, Rahab and Bathsheba, all of whom have unusual or foreign connections. She stands as Scripture's model of loyalty and of the inclusion of the nations.

traditions.text: Ruth was a descendant of Eglon, king of Moab.
Samuel wrote the book of Ruth.

voice: Gentle, modest and resolute. She speaks rarely, but when she does it is in plain, binding promises and polite, courageous requests.

names.meaning: in him is strength (uncertain); also the name of a temple pillar (1 Kgs 7:21)

events.title: Notices and protects Ruth
events.summary: He greets his reapers with a blessing, honours Ruth's loyalty, invites her to eat, and has extra grain dropped for her.

events.title: Agrees to redeem at the threshing floor
events.summary: Startled awake at midnight, he blesses Ruth, promises to act as redeemer if the nearer kinsman will not, and sends her home with grain.

events.title: Redeems the land and marries Ruth
events.summary: Before ten elders at the gate, the nearer redeemer declines and hands over his sandal, and Boaz acquires the land and Ruth. Obed is born.

summary: Boaz of Bethlehem, 'a mighty man of wealth' of Elimelech's clan, is the generous landowner who protects the foreign widow Ruth and, as kinsman-redeemer, marries her to preserve the name and inheritance of her dead husband. His conduct embodies the covenant law's care for the poor and the stranger, and his willingness to redeem at cost to himself makes him, for Christian readers, a picture of Christ. Matthew names him as the son of Rahab, although many think the genealogy is compressed.
textSays: He was a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech. He blessed his workers, protected and provided for Ruth, agreed to act as redeemer, settled the matter before elders at the gate, married Ruth, and fathered Obed. Matthew 1:5 calls him son of Salmon and Rahab.

interpretations.view: Some rabbis identify Boaz with the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem (Judg 12:8-10). They praise his self-control at the threshing floor.
Boaz as go'el is a classic type of Christ the Redeemer, who takes a Gentile bride and pays the price of redemption.

traditions.text: Boaz is the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem.

voice: Courteous, warm and dignified, an older man of standing who blesses freely. He is meticulous about doing things properly.

events.title: Born and named by the women of Bethlehem
events.summary: Born to Ruth and Boaz, he is nursed by Naomi and named by the neighbour women, who call him a restorer of life to her.

summary: Obed, son of Boaz and the Moabite Ruth, was the father of Jesse and grandfather of King David. He appears only at the end of Ruth and in genealogies, but the women's blessing of him as a 'restorer of life' and the line that follows him give the book its climax: through a foreign widow's loyalty God prepares Israel's royal house.
textSays: He was born to Ruth and Boaz, nursed by Naomi, named by the neighbour women, and fathered Jesse.

interpretations.view: He is the link that connects the faithful outsider Ruth to David and so to Christ (Matt 1:5).

voice: Quiet and unassuming, a man who knows he stands in someone else's story.

events.title: Samuel anoints his youngest son
events.summary: Samuel comes to Jesse's sacrifice. After seven sons are passed over, the youngest, David, is fetched from the sheep and anointed.

events.title: Sends David to his brothers at the front
events.summary: Now old, he sends David with provisions to his three eldest sons in Saul's army.

events.title: Sheltered in Moab
events.summary: During David's flight from Saul, Jesse and his wife are placed under the protection of the king of Moab.

summary: Jesse of Bethlehem, grandson of Ruth and Boaz, was the father of eight sons, the youngest of whom, David, was anointed king by Samuel. He is otherwise a background figure. His name lives on chiefly through prophecy: Isaiah foresees 'a rod out of the stem of Jesse', a royal shoot from the cut-down line of David. The New Testament applies this image to Christ, and Christian art developed it into the 'Jesse Tree'.
textSays: He was son of Obed and father of eight sons (seven named in 1 Chronicles 2) and two daughters. He hosted Samuel, sent David to Saul and to the front, and took refuge in Moab during David's outlaw years. Isaiah prophesies a shoot and root of Jesse.

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition counts Jesse among four people who died only because of the serpent's sin, not their own (b. Shabbat 55b). The 'stem of Jesse' is read messianically.
The 'root of Jesse' is fulfilled in Christ (Rom 15:12; Rev 5:5 speaks of the Root of David). Medieval art and Advent practice depict the Jesse Tree from Jesse to Jesus.

voice: An old, plain Bethlehem farmer, proud of his strong elder sons and slow to think of the youngest.
